english_text:
Heading: What ال does
Arabic has no word for “a” or “an”. A noun is indefinite by default and usually ends in tanween (ـٌ, ـً or ـٍ): كِتَابٌ means “a book”.
To say “the book”, attach ال to the front of the noun and replace the tanween with a single short vowel: الْكِتَابُ. The article is always written joined to the noun, never as a separate word, and it never changes for masculine, feminine or plural nouns.

english_text:
Heading: Moon letters: the lam is pronounced
If the noun begins with one of the 14 moon letters (الْحُرُوفُ الْقَمَرِيَّةُ), the lam of ال is pronounced clearly and carries a sukun: الْقَمَرُ is “al-qamaru”.
The moon letters are: ا ب ج ح خ ع غ ف ق ك م ه و ي. The first one, alif, stands for words that begin with a hamza, such as الْأَبُ (“the father”).

Heading: Sun letters: the lam is silent
If the noun begins with one of the 14 sun letters (الْحُرُوفُ الشَّمْسِيَّةُ), the lam of ال is not pronounced. Instead the first letter of the noun is doubled, and Arabic shows this with a shadda: الشَّمْسُ is “ash-shamsu”, not “al-shamsu”.
The sun letters are: ت ث د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن. All of them are made with the front of the tongue, which is why the lam blends into them. The lam is still written; only the pronunciation changes.

english_text:
Heading: The alif of ال after another word
When another word comes just before ال, the alif of ال is not pronounced. أَيْنَ الْمِفْتَاحُ؟ is said “ayna l-miftāḥu?” and فِي الْبَيْتِ is said “fī l-bayti”. At the very start of a sentence you do say the alif: “al-kitābu”.
In this course the transliteration shows this silent alif with a hyphen after the l: l-miftāḥu.

Heading: Definite and indefinite endings
A noun with ال never takes tanween. The tanween becomes a plain short vowel: بَيْتٌ (a house) becomes الْبَيْتُ (the house). Never write الْبَيْتٌ.

Heading: Guided practice: make “the pen” and “the car”
Step 1 — Start with the indefinite words: قَلَمٌ (a pen) and سَيَّارَةٌ (a car).
Step 2 — Remove the tanween and use a plain damma: قَلَمُ and سَيَّارَةُ.
Step 3 — Look at the first letter. ق is a moon letter, so the lam is pronounced and has a sukun: الْقَلَمُ (al-qalamu).
Step 4 — س is a sun letter, so the lam is silent and the س gets a shadda: السَّيَّارَةُ (as-sayyāratu).
Remember: the lam carries a sukun only before moon letters.

lesson_title: Definite article: sun and moon letters
field: explanation block (heading and text)
english_text:
Heading: Lesson review
• ال means “the” and is always joined to the noun.
• Before a moon letter the lam is pronounced (al-). Before a sun letter it is silent and the next letter is doubled (ash-, an-, ad-, as-…).
• There are 14 of each kind. Learn the sun letters first: every other letter is a moon letter.
• After another word, the alif of ال is not pronounced (l-).
• A noun with ال has no tanween.

english_text:
Heading: The six pronouns
أَنَا (anā) — I
أَنْتَ (anta) — you, said to a man
أَنْتِ (anti) — you, said to a woman
هُوَ (huwa) — he
هِيَ (hiya) — she
نَحْنُ (naḥnu) — we
Arabic also has dual and plural forms (for example “they” and “you all”); they are not covered in this lesson. Notice that “you” has two forms and only the last vowel changes: a fatha for a man (anta), a kasra for a woman (anti).

english_text:
Heading: No word for “am”, “is” or “are”
In ordinary present-tense sentences Arabic does not use a word for “am/is/are”. You simply put the two parts side by side: the subject (الْمُبْتَدَأُ) and what is said about it (الْخَبَرُ).
أَنَا مُهَنْدِسٌ literally means “I engineer”, and it is translated “I am an engineer”. (It is the same “I am a …” pattern that you met in the sentence patterns.) Sentences like this are called nominal sentences (الْجُمْلَةُ الِاسْمِيَّةُ) because they begin with a noun or a pronoun, not with a verb.

Heading: How ة is pronounced
ة (taa marbuta, “tied taa”) appears only at the end of a word and looks like ه with two dots. Its sound depends on what follows:
• At the end of a sentence, or when you read without case endings, it sounds like a short “a” (or a soft “h”): مَدْرَسَة is “madrasa”.
• When an ending or another word follows, it becomes a “t”: مَدْرَسَةٌ is “madrasatun”, and مَدْرَسَةُ الْبِنْتِ is “madrasatu l-binti”.
Do not confuse it with the ordinary letter ت, which is always pronounced “t”.

english_text:
Heading: Where the adjective goes
In Arabic the adjective comes after the noun it describes: بَيْتٌ كَبِيرٌ is “a big house” (literally “a house big”).
The adjective must agree with the noun in gender, in definiteness and in its case ending. In this course you will mostly see the first two.

Heading: Gender
A feminine noun takes a feminine adjective, made by adding ة: مَدْرَسَةٌ كَبِيرَةٌ (a big school), سَيَّارَةٌ جَدِيدَةٌ (a new car).
A masculine noun takes the masculine form: كِتَابٌ جَدِيدٌ (a new book), بَيْتٌ صَغِيرٌ (a small house).

english_text:
Heading: Definiteness
If the noun is indefinite, the adjective is indefinite: بَيْتٌ كَبِيرٌ. If the noun has ال, the adjective also gets ال: الْبَيْتُ الْكَبِيرُ (“the big house”).
The adjective copies both the ال and the ending of the noun: الْمَدْرَسَةُ الْكَبِيرَةُ.

english_text:
Heading: Phrase or sentence?
Compare these three:
بَيْتٌ كَبِيرٌ — a big house (a phrase)
الْبَيْتُ الْكَبِيرُ — the big house (a phrase)
الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ — the house is big (a complete sentence)
When both words have ال, you have a phrase. When only the noun has ال and the adjective has none, the adjective is what you say about the noun: a sentence, with no word for “is” (lesson 2).

Heading: Two nouns side by side
Arabic shows possession by putting two nouns next to each other. The owned thing comes first and the owner second: كِتَابُ الطَّالِبِ is “the book of the student”, that is, “the student’s book”.
This is called الْإِضَافَةُ (idāfa, “annexation”). The first noun is الْمُضَافُ and the second is الْمُضَافُ إِلَيْهِ.

Heading: Three rules
1. The first noun never has ال and never has tanween.
2. The second noun usually has ال (or is a name) and ends in a kasra (ـِ), the “of” ending: الطَّالِبِ.
3. The two nouns work as one unit, so nothing can come between them. The first noun’s own ending depends on its job in the sentence; as a subject it has a damma: كِتَابُ الطَّالِبِ جَدِيدٌ.
If the second noun has no ال, the whole phrase is indefinite: كِتَابُ طَالِبٍ is “a student’s book”.

english_text:
Heading: How the present tense works
The Arabic present tense (الْمُضَارِعُ) is made by adding a prefix to a verb stem, and sometimes an ending. The prefix shows who is doing the action. One form covers both “I write” and “I am writing”.
Dictionaries list a verb by its “he did” form (كَتَبَ, “he wrote”), so be careful: that form is the past tense, not the present.

english_text:
Heading: The pattern for كَتَبَ (“to write”)
The stem is ـكْتُبـ (-ktub-):
أَنَا أَكْتُبُ — I write (prefix أَـ)
أَنْتَ تَكْتُبُ — you write, to a man (prefix تَـ)
أَنْتِ تَكْتُبِينَ — you write, to a woman (prefix تَـ and ending ـِينَ)
هُوَ يَكْتُبُ — he writes (prefix يَـ)
هِيَ تَكْتُبُ — she writes (prefix تَـ)
نَحْنُ نَكْتُبُ — we write (prefix نَـ)
The forms for “you (to a man)” and “she” look the same. The pronoun, or the situation, tells you which one is meant.

Heading: The stem vowel
In these verbs the first stem letter has a sukun, and the vowel on the middle letter depends on the verb. You learn it with each verb: كَتَبَ → يَكْتُبُ (damma), ذَهَبَ → يَذْهَبُ (fatha), شَرِبَ → يَشْرَبُ (fatha). The prefixes and the ending ـِينَ are the same for all three.

Heading: Endings and pronouns
In a normal statement the present-tense verb ends in a damma (ـُ), as in أَكْتُبُ. The only special ending in this lesson is ـِينَ for “you (to a woman)”. Real Arabic often drops the pronoun, because أَكْتُبُ already means “I write”; it is kept here so you can see who is acting.

Heading: Objects and prepositions
A direct object takes a fatha ending: أَنَا أَكْتُبُ الدَّرْسَ (“I write the lesson”). A noun after a preposition such as إِلَى (“to”) takes a kasra: أَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَةِ (“I go to school”). Prepositions are explained in lesson 8.

Heading: Verb-first sentences
Arabic sentences often begin with the verb: يَكْتُبُ الطَّالِبُ الدَّرْسَ (“The student writes the lesson”). The verb comes first, so it uses the singular “he” form (يَكْتُبُ), and the subject follows with a damma (الطَّالِبُ). This is a verbal sentence (الْجُمْلَةُ الْفِعْلِيَّةُ), in contrast to the nominal sentences of lesson 2.
The order pronoun + verb that you practise in this lesson (أَنَا أَكْتُبُ) is also correct and keeps the person easy to see.

Heading: The ending after لَيْسَ
After لَيْسَ, the word that says what the subject is (or is like) takes a fatha ending, usually written as tanween fatha with an alif: أَنَا مُهَنْدِسٌ becomes لَسْتُ مُهَنْدِسًا. Heading: Prepositions
Prepositions are short words that go before a noun:
فِي — in, at
عَلَى — on

Heading: Do not mix them up
